title: Part 5, Chapter 2
paragraphs: It would be hard to explain exactly what gave rise to the idea of that senseless dinner in Katerina Ivanovna's disordered mind. Nearly ten of the twenty rubles Raskolnikov had given for Marmeladov's funeral were squandered on it. Perhaps Katerina Ivanovna felt obligated to honor the dead man's memory "properly," so that all the lodgers, and especially Amalia Ivanovna, would see that "he was by no means inferior to them, and perhaps quite their superior," and that no one had the right "to look down on him." Perhaps the main factor was that peculiar poor-man's pride that compels so many destitute people to spend their last savings on some traditional social ritual, simply to be "like everyone else" and not "give anyone reason to despise them." Quite likely, too, Katerina Ivanovna longed to show on this particular occasion -- when she seemed abandoned by everyone -- that those "miserable, contemptible lodgers" should know "she understood how things were done, how to entertain," and that she had been raised "in a genteel, one might almost say an aristocratic colonel's family" and had not been destined for sweeping floors and washing the children's rags at night. Even the poorest, most broken-spirited people are sometimes seized by these fits of pride and vanity that take the form of an irresistible, nervous compulsion. And Katerina Ivanovna was not broken in spirit; circumstances might have killed her, but her spirit could never be crushed -- she could never be intimidated, her will could never be broken. Besides, Sonia had said with good reason that her mind was becoming unhinged. She couldn't exactly be called insane, but for the past year she had been under such relentless pressure that her mind might well have been strained past its limits. The later stages of tuberculosis, doctors say, tend to affect the brain.

The selection of wines was not impressive, and there was no Madeira; but wine there was. There was vodka, rum, and Lisbon wine, all of the cheapest quality but in decent quantities. Besides the traditional rice and honey dish, there were three or four other courses, one of them pancakes, all prepared in Amalia Ivanovna's kitchen. Two samovars were set up so that tea and punch could be offered after dinner. Katerina Ivanovna had done the shopping herself, with the help of one of the lodgers -- a wretched little Pole who had somehow ended up stranded at Madame Lippevechsel's. He had immediately put himself at Katerina Ivanovna's disposal and had spent all the previous day and all that morning running about with his legs barely keeping up, very anxious that everyone should notice his efforts. At every trifle he dashed back to Katerina Ivanovna, even tracking her down at the market, and constantly called her "Pani." By the end she was thoroughly sick of him, though at first she had proclaimed that without this "helpful and generous man" she couldn't have managed at all. It was one of Katerina Ivanovna's traits to paint everyone she met in the most glowing colors. Her praises were so extravagant as to be embarrassing; she would invent flattering details about a new acquaintance and believe them with perfect sincerity. Then just as suddenly she would become disillusioned and rudely, contemptuously cast off the person she had been literally worshiping only hours before. She was by nature cheerful, lively, and peace-loving, but endless failures and misfortunes had made her crave so desperately that everyone live in peace and joy and not dare to disturb it, that the slightest upset, the smallest misfortune, would drive her nearly to frenzy, and in an instant she would plunge from the brightest hopes and fantasies to cursing her fate and raving and banging her head against the wall.

Amalia Ivanovna, too, had suddenly risen enormously in Katerina Ivanovna's estimation and was treated with extraordinary respect -- probably only because she had thrown herself wholeheartedly into the preparations. She had volunteered to lay the table, provide the linens and crockery, and cook the dishes in her kitchen, and Katerina Ivanovna had left everything in her hands and gone off to the cemetery. Everything had turned out quite well: the tablecloth was nearly clean, and although the crockery, knives, forks, and glasses were of every possible shape and pattern, borrowed from various lodgers, the table was properly set by the appointed time. Amalia Ivanovna, feeling she had done her work well, had put on a black silk dress and a cap with new mourning ribbons and greeted the returning party with some pride. This pride, though justified, annoyed Katerina Ivanovna: "As if the table couldn't have been laid without Amalia Ivanovna!" She disliked the cap with its new ribbons too. "Was this stupid German putting on airs because she was the landlady and had agreed as a favor to help her poor lodgers? As a favor! Imagine! Katerina Ivanovna's father, who had been a colonel and practically a governor, sometimes set the table for forty guests, and a person like Amalia Ivanovna -- or rather, Ludwigovna -- wouldn't even have been allowed into the kitchen."

Katerina Ivanovna kept these feelings to herself for the moment, though she resolved that she would certainly have to put Amalia Ivanovna in her place and remind her of her proper station, since God only knew what the woman was starting to imagine. She was also irritated that hardly any of the invited lodgers had come to the funeral -- only the Pole, who had barely made it to the cemetery -- while at the memorial dinner, the most pathetic and insignificant of them had turned up, many not entirely sober. The older, more respectable lodgers had all stayed away, as though by prior agreement. Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin, for example, who might be called the most respectable lodger of all, had not appeared, although the evening before, Katerina Ivanovna had told the whole world -- meaning Amalia Ivanovna, Polenka, Sonia, and the Pole -- that he was the most generous, noble-hearted man, with a large fortune and vast connections, who had been a friend of her first husband and a guest in her father's home, and who had promised to use all his influence to obtain her a substantial pension. It should be noted that when Katerina Ivanovna praised someone's connections and fortune, she did it without any ulterior motive, quite disinterestedly, for the sheer pleasure of enhancing the person's stature. Probably "following Luzhin's lead," "that contemptible wretch Lebeziatnikov hadn't shown up either. What did he think he was? He'd only been invited as a courtesy, because he shared a room with Pyotr Petrovitch and was his friend, so it would have been awkward not to ask him."

Among those who failed to appear were "the genteel lady and her spinster daughter," who had been lodgers for only about two weeks but had complained several times about noise and commotion from Katerina Ivanovna's quarters, especially when Marmeladov came home drunk. Katerina Ivanovna had heard this from Amalia Ivanovna, who, during a quarrel, had threatened to throw the whole family out, shouting that they "weren't worth the foot" of the respectable lodgers they were disturbing. Katerina Ivanovna now made it a point to invite this lady and her daughter, "whose foot she wasn't worth," and who had turned away haughtily when they passed her, so they would see that "her thoughts and feelings were more noble" and that "she harbored no malice," and understand that she was not accustomed to living this way. She intended to make this clear through references to her late father's quasi-governorship, while hinting that it was extremely foolish of them to snub her. The stout retired major (actually a discharged low-ranking officer) was also absent, having apparently been "not himself" for the past two days. The actual guests consisted of the little Pole; a pathetic-looking clerk with a pimply face and a greasy coat, who had nothing to say for himself and smelled abominably; a deaf and nearly blind old man who had once worked at the post office and whom someone at Amalia Ivanovna's had been supporting for ages.

A retired clerk from the commissariat department also came -- he was drunk, had a loud and extremely unseemly laugh, and -- can you imagine -- was wearing no waistcoat! One guest sat down at the table without even greeting Katerina Ivanovna. One person, having no proper suit, attempted to come in his dressing gown, but this was too much, and the combined efforts of Amalia Ivanovna and the Pole succeeded in removing him. The Pole, however, brought along two other Poles who didn't live at Amalia Ivanovna's and whom no one had ever seen there before. All of this infuriated Katerina Ivanovna. "Who had she made all these preparations for?" To make room for the guests, the children hadn't even been given places at the table. Instead, the two younger ones sat on a trunk in the far corner, their food set on a box in front of them, while Polenka, as the eldest, was expected to look after them, feed them, and keep their noses wiped "like well-bred children."

In fact, Katerina Ivanovna could hardly help receiving her guests with heightened dignity, even haughtiness. She fixed certain individuals with a severe stare, then loftily invited them to sit down. Having decided for some reason that Amalia Ivanovna must be to blame for the missing guests, she began treating her with extreme disdain, which the landlady immediately noticed and deeply resented. Such a beginning did not bode well for the end. At last everyone was seated.

Raskolnikov arrived at almost the same moment as the group returned from the cemetery. Katerina Ivanovna was delighted to see him, first because he was the one "educated guest, and everyone knew he was two years from becoming a university professor," and second because he immediately and respectfully apologized for having missed the funeral. She pounced on him and seated him at her left (Amalia Ivanovna was on her right). Despite her constant anxiety about the dishes being passed correctly and everyone tasting them, and despite the agonizing cough that interrupted her every minute and seemed to have worsened in recent days, she hastened to pour out in a half-whisper all her pent-up feelings and righteous indignation over the failed dinner, interspersing her complaints with lively, uncontrollable laughter at the expense of her guests and especially her landlady.

"It's all that cuckoo's fault! You know who I mean -- her, her!" Katerina Ivanovna nodded toward the landlady. "Look at her making big eyes -- she can tell we're talking about her but can't understand a word. The owl! Ha-ha! (Cough-cough-cough.) And what does she think she's doing in that cap? (Cough-cough-cough.) Have you noticed she wants everyone to think she's doing me a favor, gracing us with her presence? I asked her, like a sensible woman, to invite people, especially those who knew my late husband, and look at the collection of fools she's dragged in! The janitors! Look at that one with the pimply face. And those wretched Poles -- ha-ha-ha! (Cough-cough-cough.) Not one of them has ever set foot in here before. I've never laid eyes on them. What are they doing here, I ask you? There they sit in a row. Hey, pan!" she shouted suddenly at one of them, "have you tried the pancakes? Take some more! Have some beer! Won't you have vodka? Look, he's jumped up and bowing -- they must be half-starved, poor things. Well, let them eat! At least they're quiet. Though I am worried about the landlady's silver spoons... Amalia Ivanovna!" she said suddenly, almost aloud, "if your spoons happen to go missing, I won't be held responsible, I'm warning you! Ha-ha-ha!" She laughed, turning to Raskolnikov and nodding at the landlady again, delighted with her own wit. "She doesn't understand, she doesn't understand again! Look at her sitting there with her mouth hanging open! An owl -- a real owl! An owl in new ribbons, ha-ha-ha!"

Her laugh dissolved into an unbearable coughing fit that lasted five minutes. Drops of sweat stood on her forehead, and her handkerchief was spotted with blood. She silently showed the blood to Raskolnikov and, as soon as she could catch her breath, began whispering to him again with feverish animation, a hectic flush burning in her cheeks.

"You see, I gave her the most delicate instructions -- the most exquisite tact, you might say -- for inviting that lady and her daughter. You know who I mean? It required the utmost finesse, the greatest subtlety, but she handled it so badly that that fool, that conceited nobody, that provincial nonentity -- simply because she's the widow of a major and has come here to pester government offices about a pension and wear out her skirts in waiting rooms -- because at fifty she paints her face (everybody knows it) -- a creature like that didn't see fit to come and hasn't even responded to the invitation, which common decency required! I can't understand why Pyotr Petrovitch hasn't come either. But where's Sonia? Where did she go? Ah, there she is at last! What is it, Sonia -- where have you been? It's odd to be late even to your father's funeral. Rodion Romanovitch, make room for her beside you. That's your place, Sonia... take what you like. Have some of the cold appetizer with aspic -- that's the best. They'll bring the pancakes in a moment. Have the children been served? Polenka, do you have everything? (Cough-cough-cough.) Good. Be a good girl, Lida, and Kolya -- stop fidgeting with your feet. Sit like a little gentleman. What were you saying, Sonia?"

Sonia hastened to relay Pyotr Petrovitch's apologies, trying to speak loudly enough for everyone to hear and carefully using the most respectful phrases, which she attributed to Pyotr Petrovitch himself. She added that he had specifically asked her to say that as soon as possible he would come to discuss business with her privately and to consider what might be done for her, and so on.

Sonia knew this would comfort Katerina Ivanovna, would flatter and gratify her pride. She sat down beside Raskolnikov, gave him a quick bow, and glanced at him with fleeting curiosity. But for the rest of the time she seemed to avoid looking at him or speaking to him. She appeared distracted, though she kept watching Katerina Ivanovna, trying to please her. Neither she nor Katerina Ivanovna had been able to get mourning clothes. Sonia wore dark brown, and Katerina Ivanovna had on her only dress, a dark striped cotton one.

The message from Pyotr Petrovitch was a great success. Listening to Sonia with dignity, Katerina Ivanovna inquired with equal dignity about Pyotr Petrovitch's health, then immediately whispered almost aloud to Raskolnikov that it would certainly have been strange for a man of Pyotr Petrovitch's position and standing to find himself in such "extraordinary company," despite his devotion to her family and his old friendship with her father.

"That's why I'm so grateful to you, Rodion Romanovitch, for not disdaining my hospitality, even in such surroundings," she added, almost aloud. "But I'm sure it was only your special feeling for my poor husband that made you keep your promise."

Then, with renewed pride and dignity, she surveyed her guests and suddenly asked the deaf old man across the table in a loud voice whether he'd like more meat and whether he'd been given wine. The old man didn't answer and for a long time couldn't understand what was being asked, though his neighbors amused themselves by poking and shaking him. He simply stared around with his mouth open, which only increased the general hilarity.

"What an imbecile! Look at him! Why did they bring him? But as for Pyotr Petrovitch, I always had confidence in him," Katerina Ivanovna continued, addressing Amalia Ivanovna in such a sharp, loud voice that the landlady was taken aback, "not like your overdressed trollops, whom my father wouldn't have taken on as kitchen maids, and whom my late husband honored simply by inviting them, out of the goodness of his heart."
"Yes, he was fond of the drink, he was -- he certainly drank!" the commissariat clerk shouted, tossing back his twelfth glass of vodka.

"My late husband certainly had that weakness, and everyone knows it," Katerina Ivanovna pounced at once. "But he was a kind and honorable man who loved and respected his family. The trouble was that his good nature made him trust all sorts of disreputable people, and he drank with fellows who weren't worth the soles of his shoes. Would you believe it, Rodion Romanovitch -- they found a gingerbread rooster in his pocket! He was dead drunk, but he didn't forget the children!"
"A rooster? Did you say a rooster?" the commissariat clerk bellowed.
Katerina Ivanovna did not deign to reply. She sighed, lost in thought.

"No doubt you think, like everyone else, that I was too hard on him," she went on, addressing Raskolnikov. "But that's not true! He respected me -- he respected me deeply! He was kind-hearted! And how I pitied him sometimes! He'd sit in a corner and look at me, and I'd feel such pity for him, such an urge to be gentle -- and then I'd think: 'Be gentle with him and he'll start drinking again.' Strictness was the only thing that kept him in line."
"Yes, he got his hair pulled often enough!" roared the commissariat clerk, downing another glass.
"Some fools could use a good thrashing along with the hair-pulling. And I'm not talking about my late husband now!" Katerina Ivanovna snapped at him.

The flush on her cheeks deepened, her chest heaved. Another minute and she would have caused a scene. Many of the guests were snickering, clearly delighted. They began poking the commissariat clerk and whispering to him, obviously trying to egg him on.
"Allow me -- what exactly are you referring to?" the clerk began. "That is to say, whose -- about whom were you -- but never mind! Nonsense! A widow! I forgive you... I pass!"
And he drained another glass of vodka.

Raskolnikov sat in silence, listening with disgust. He ate only out of politeness, barely tasting the food that Katerina Ivanovna kept heaping on his plate, so as not to hurt her feelings. He watched Sonia intently. But Sonia grew more and more anxious and distressed; she too could see that the dinner would not end peacefully, and she watched Katerina Ivanovna's mounting irritation with dread. She knew that she, Sonia, was the main reason the "genteel" ladies had treated Katerina Ivanovna's invitation with contempt. She had heard from Amalia Ivanovna that the mother had been positively offended and had asked: "How could she seat her daughter next to that young woman?" Sonia sensed that Katerina Ivanovna had already found out about this, and an insult to Sonia meant more to Katerina Ivanovna than an insult to herself, her children, or her father. Sonia knew Katerina Ivanovna would not rest "until she had shown those trollops." To make things worse, someone at the far end of the table passed Sonia a plate with two hearts pierced by an arrow, cut from black bread. Katerina Ivanovna flushed crimson and immediately declared across the table that the sender was "a drunken jackass."

Amalia Ivanovna, sensing something unpleasant in the air and at the same time deeply offended by Katerina Ivanovna's haughtiness, attempted to restore the mood and raise herself in the company's estimation by suddenly, apropos of nothing, telling a story about an acquaintance of hers, "Karl from the chemist's," who was taking a cab one night, and "the cabman wanted him to kill, and Karl very much begged him not to kill, and wept and clasped his hands, and was frightened and from fear his heart was pierced." Although Katerina Ivanovna smiled, she immediately observed that Amalia Ivanovna really shouldn't attempt to tell anecdotes in Russian. The landlady took even greater offense and retorted that her "Vater aus Berlin was a very important man and always walked with his hands in his pockets." Katerina Ivanovna laughed so hard that Amalia Ivanovna nearly lost all patience.

"Listen to the owl!" Katerina Ivanovna whispered, her good humor almost restored. "She meant to say he kept his hands in his pockets, but she said he put his hands in people's pockets. (Cough-cough.) And have you noticed, Rodion Romanovitch, that all these Petersburg foreigners, especially the Germans, are stupider than us? Can you imagine anyone telling how 'Karl from the chemist's' had 'his heart pierced from fear' -- and that the idiot, instead of punishing the cabman, 'clasped his hands and wept and begged very much'? And she thinks it's terribly touching and doesn't even realize how stupid it is! To my mind, that drunken commissariat clerk is far more clever -- at least you can see he's drunk his brains away. But these foreigners are always so prim and serious... Look at her glaring! She's angry, ha-ha! (Cough-cough-cough.)"

Her mood restored, Katerina Ivanovna immediately launched into telling Raskolnikov that once she obtained her pension, she intended to open a boarding school for young ladies of good family in her native town of T----. This was the first time she had mentioned the plan to him, and she plunged into the most enchanting details. Somehow the very certificate of honor that Marmeladov had told Raskolnikov about in the tavern -- the one proving that Katerina Ivanovna had danced the shawl dance before the governor and other dignitaries upon finishing school -- suddenly appeared in her hands. This certificate was obviously meant to prove Katerina Ivanovna's right to open a boarding school, but it had been brought out mainly to crush "those two stuck-up trollops" should they appear, proving beyond doubt that Katerina Ivanovna came from "the most noble, one might even say aristocratic family, a colonel's daughter, and was far superior to certain adventuresses who have been so prominent lately." The certificate was immediately passed around among the drunken guests, and Katerina Ivanovna made no effort to hold on to it, since it actually stated in black and white that her father had held the rank of major and was also a companion of an order, making her practically a colonel's daughter.

Warming to her theme, Katerina Ivanovna elaborated on the peaceful, happy life they would lead in T----, on the high school teachers she would hire for her boarding school -- one of them a most respectable old Frenchman named Mangot, who had taught Katerina Ivanovna herself in her youth and was still living in T----, where he would no doubt accept a teaching position on reasonable terms. Next she spoke of Sonia, who would go with her to T---- and assist in all her plans. At this, someone at the far end of the table let out a sudden guffaw.

Though Katerina Ivanovna tried to appear disdainfully unaware of the laughter, she immediately raised her voice and began speaking with conviction about Sonia's undoubted ability to assist her, about "her gentleness, patience, devotion, generosity, and fine education," patting Sonia on the cheek and kissing her warmly twice. Sonia blushed crimson. Katerina Ivanovna suddenly burst into tears, immediately declaring that she was "being silly and emotional, that she was too overwrought, that it was time to stop, and since dinner was over, it was time to serve the tea."

At that moment, Amalia Ivanovna, deeply aggrieved at being excluded from the conversation, made one last effort and, with some trepidation, ventured an extremely weighty observation: that "in the future boarding school she would need to pay particular attention to die Wasche" and that "there certainly must be a good dame to look after the linen," and secondly that "the young ladies must not novels at night read."

Katerina Ivanovna, who was certainly upset and very tired, and thoroughly sick of the dinner, immediately cut her short, saying "she knew nothing about it and was talking nonsense, that it was the laundry maid's business to look after die Wasche, not the directress of a distinguished boarding school, and as for novel-reading, that was simply rude, and she begged her to be quiet." Amalia Ivanovna flared up and, getting angry, declared that she had only "meant her good" and that "she had meant her very good," and that "it was a long time since she had been paid her gold for the lodgings."

Katerina Ivanovna immediately "put her in her place," saying it was a lie that she wished her well, because just yesterday, while her dead husband was lying on the table, she had been hounding her about the rent. To this, Amalia Ivanovna very aptly replied that she had invited those ladies, but "those ladies did not come, because those ladies are ladies and cannot come to a lady who is not a lady." Katerina Ivanovna pointed out that, being a slut, Amalia Ivanovna was hardly in a position to judge what made a real lady. Amalia Ivanovna declared that her "Vater aus Berlin was a very, very important man and both hands in pockets went and always said 'Poof! Poof!'" and she leapt from the table to demonstrate her father, stuffing her hands in her pockets, puffing out her cheeks, and making vague sounds like "poof! poof!" to great laughter from the lodgers, who deliberately encouraged her, hoping for a fight.

But this was too much for Katerina Ivanovna, and she announced in a voice for all to hear that Amalia Ivanovna probably never had a father at all, that she was just some drunken Petersburg Finn who had no doubt once been a cook "and probably something worse." Amalia Ivanovna turned red as a lobster and shrieked that perhaps Katerina Ivanovna never had a father either, "but she had a Vater aus Berlin who wore a long coat and always said poof-poof-poof!"

Katerina Ivanovna remarked contemptuously that her family background was well known and that on that very certificate of honor it was printed that her father had been a colonel, while Amalia Ivanovna's father -- if she even had one -- was probably some Finnish milkman, though more likely she never had a father at all, since it remained unclear whether her name was Amalia Ivanovna or Amalia Ludwigovna.

At this, Amalia Ivanovna, driven to fury, pounded the table with her fist and screamed that she was Amalia Ivanovna, not Ludwigovna, "that her Vater was called Johann and was a burgomaster, and that Katerina Ivanovna's Vater was never at all a burgomaster." Katerina Ivanovna rose from her chair and, in a stern, apparently calm voice -- though she was white-faced and her chest was heaving -- declared that "if she dared for one moment to put her wretched father on the same level as her papa, she, Katerina Ivanovna, would tear the cap off her head and trample it underfoot." Amalia Ivanovna began running around the room, shouting at the top of her lungs that she was the landlady and Katerina Ivanovna must vacate the premises immediately; then she rushed to collect the silver spoons from the table. A tremendous uproar ensued; the children began to wail. Sonia rushed to restrain Katerina Ivanovna, but when Amalia Ivanovna shouted something about "the yellow ticket," Katerina Ivanovna shoved Sonia aside and lunged at the landlady to carry out her threat.
At that very moment the door opened, and Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin appeared on the threshold. He stood surveying the scene with severe, watchful eyes. Katerina Ivanovna rushed toward him.
